content.content: A plasmid found in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae and used as the basis for a series of cloning vectors.
One of the two ends of a polynucleotide: that which carries the hydroxyl group attached to the 3′ position of the sugar.
One of the two ends of a polynucleotide: that which carries the phosphate group attached to the 5′ position of the sugar.
Identification of putative genes by ORF scanning of a DNA sequence.
A synthetic, double‐stranded oligonucleotide used to attach sticky ends to a blunt‐ended molecule.

A virus that is unrelated to adenovirus but which is often found in the same infected tissues, because AAV makes use of some of the proteins synthesized by adenovirus in order to complete its replication cycle.
An animal virus, derivatives of which have been used to clone genes in mammalian cells.
A chromatography method that makes use of a ligand that binds a specific protein and which can therefore be used to aid purification of that protein.
The soil bacterium which, when containing the Ti plasmid, is able to form crown galls on a number of dicotyledonous plant species.
Preserved DNA from an archaeological or fossil specimen.
Attachment of an oligonucleotide to a single‐stranded DNA molecule by hybridization.
An RNA molecule that is the reverse complement of a naturally occurring mRNA, and which can be used to prevent translation of that mRNA in a transformed cell.
The use of DNA analysis to study the human past.
Construction of an artificial gene from a series of overlapping oligonucleotides.
A method of detecting radioactively labelled molecules through exposure of an X‐ray‐sensitive photographic film.
A mutant microorganism that grows only when supplied with a nutrient not required by the wild type.
Gene Cloning and DNA Analysis: An Introduction, Eighth Edition. T. A. Brown.
© 2021 John Wiley & Sons Ltd. Published 2021 by John Wiley & Sons Ltd.
A protein that has a high affinity for biotin and is used in a detection system for biotinylated probes.
A modified baculovirus that carries a mammalian promoter and so is able to express a cloned gene directly in a mammalian cell.
A cloning vector based on the F plasmid, used for cloning relatively large fragments of DNA in E. coli.
A virus whose host is a bacterium. Bacteriophage DNA molecules are often used as cloning vectors.
A virus that has been used as a cloning vector for the production of recombinant protein in insect cells.
The oligonucleotides used to capture DNA fragments during target enrichment, prior to preparation of a next‐generation DNA sequencing library.
An enzyme capable of changing one nucleotide to another within a DNA molecule.
Growth of bacteria in a fixed volume of liquid medium in a closed vessel, with no additions or removals made during the period of incubation.
The use of computer methods in studies of genomes.
A means of introducing DNA into cells that involves bombardment with high‐velocity microprojectiles coated with DNA.

One of the precautionary measures taken to prevent the replication of recombinant DNA molecules in microorganisms in the natural environment. Biological containment involves the use of vectors and host organisms that have been modified so that they will not survive outside the laboratory.
The use of biological processes in industry and technology.
A molecule that can be incorporated into dUTP and used as a nonradioactive label for a DNA probe.
An algorithm frequently used in homology searching.
An end of a DNA molecule at which both strands terminate at the same nucleotide position with no single‐stranded extension.
A plasmid that can replicate in a variety of host species.
Growth of microorganisms in a liquid medium.
The density possessed by a molecule or particle when suspended in an aqueous salt or sugar solution.
A gene, identified by positional cloning, that might be a disease‐causing or disease‐susceptibility gene.
A method for studying the composition of a transcriptome.
The protein coat that encloses the DNA or RNA molecule of a bacteriophage or virus.
The chemical modification at the 5´‐end of most eukaryotic mRNA molecules.
A programmable nuclease that is directed to its target site by a 20‐nucleotide guide RNA.

A DNA sequence consisting of promoter–ribosome‐binding site– single‐copy restriction site–terminator (or for a eukaryotic host, promoter– single‐copy restriction site–polyadenylation sequence) carried by certain
types of expression vector. A foreign gene inserted into the restriction site is placed under control of the expression signals.

The best studied of the caulimoviruses, used in the past as a cloning vector for some species of higher plant. Cauliflower mosaic virus is the source of strong promoters used in other types of plant cloning vector.
One of the two groups of DNA viruses to infect plants, the members of which have potential as cloning vectors for some species of higher plant.
A preparation consisting of a large number of broken cells and their released contents.
A cell extract containing all the components required for protein synthesis (i.e. ribosomal subunits, tRNAs, amino acids, enzymes, and cofactors) and able to translate added mRNA molecules.
The constricted region of a chromosome that is the position at which the pair of chromatids is held together.
A chemical that interferes with the hydrogen bonding that normally holds water molecules together

(1) A recombinant DNA molecule made up of DNA fragments from more than one organism, named after the mythological beast. (2) The initial product of cloning using embryonic stem cells: an animal made up of a mixture of cells with different genotypes.
A method for identifying the positions where individual DNA‐binding proteins attach to a genome.
The DNA‐protein complex found in the nuclei of eukaryotic cells.
A method for identifying the positions where individual DNA‐binding proteins attach to a genome.
A group of techniques which achieve separation of substances by virtue of differential partitioning between mobile and stationary phases.
One of the DNA–protein structures that contains part of the nuclear genome of a eukaryote. Less accurately, the DNA molecule(s) that contains a prokaryotic genome.
A technique that can be used to construct a clone contig by identifying overlapping fragments of cloned DNA.
A cell extract that has been centrifuged to remove cell debris, subcellular particles, and possibly chromosomal DNA.
Restriction fragment length polymorphism analysis applied to a PCR product.
A population of identical cells, generally those containing identical recombinant DNA molecules.
A collection of clones whose DNA fragments overlap.
Any one of a variety of techniques that compares cloned DNA fragments in order to identify ones that overlap.
Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)
A prokaryotic immune system that forms the basis to gene editing.
The fact that not all codons are used equally frequently in the genes of a particular organism.
A technique that reduces the number of PCRs or other analyses that must be performed by combining samples in an ordered
fashion, so that a sample giving a particular result can be identified even though that sample is not individually examined.
A research strategy that uses information obtained from the study of one genome to make inferences about the map positions and functions of genes in a second genome.
The ability of two different types of plasmid to coexist in the same cell.
A culture of bacteria that has been treated to enhance their ability to take up DNA molecules.
Two polynucleotides that can base pair to form a doublestranded molecule.
A cloning technique involving conversion of purified mRNA to DNA before insertion into a vector.
The spatial organization of a molecule. Linear and circular are two possible conformations of a polynucleotide.
Physical contact between two bacteria, usually associated with transfer of DNA from one cell to the other.

A nucleotide sequence used to describe a large number of related though non‐identical sequences. Each position of the consensus sequence represents the nucleotide most often found at that position in the real sequences.
The culture of microorganisms in liquid medium under controlled conditions, with additions to and removals from the medium over a lengthy period of time.
An electrophoresis technique for the separation of large DNA molecules.
The number of molecules of a plasmid contained in a single cell.
A cloning vector consisting of the λ cos site inserted into a plasmid, used to clone DNA fragments up to 40 kb in size.
One of the cohesive, single‐stranded extensions present at the ends of the DNA molecules of certain strains of λ phage.
A completely double‐stranded circular DNA molecule, with no nicks or discontinuities, usually with a supercoiled conformation.
The average number of reads that cover each nucleotide position in a DNA sequence obtained by a next-generation method.
A GC‐rich DNA region located upstream of 40–50% of the genes in the human genome.
A bacterial growth medium in which all the components are known.
The identification of control sequences for a gene by determining the effects on gene expression of specific deletions in the upstream region.

A segment of DNA that is transferred to a yeast chromosome by homologous recombination in order to create a deleted version of a target gene, in order to inactivate that gene and identify its function.
Of nucleic acid molecules: breakdown by chemical or physical means of the hydrogen bonds involved in base pairing.
Construction of an artificial gene from a series of overlapping oligonucleotides.
A strategy in which a genome sequence is assembled solely by finding overlaps between individual sequence reads.
Separation of molecules and particles on the basis of buoyant density, by centrifugation in a concentrated sucrose or caesium chloride solution.
A modified nucleotide that lacks the 3′ hydroxyl group and so prevents further chain elongation when incorporated into a growing polynucleotide.
A set of experimental techniques that is used to obtain novel genes with improved products.
A cloning process that involves transfer of a gene into a chromosome without the use of a cloning vector able to replicate in the host organism.
A Ti plasmid that has had some or all of the T‐DNA genes removed, so it is no longer able to promote cancerous growth of plant cells.
A wafer of silicon carrying a high‐density array of oligonucleotides used in transcriptome and other studies.
A mixture of DNA fragments, whose sizes are multiples of 100 bp or of 1 kb, used as size markers during gel electrophoresis.
An enzyme that, in the cell, repairs single‐stranded discontinuities in double‐stranded DNA molecules. Purified DNA ligase is used in gene cloning to join DNA molecules together.
A DNA sequence that exists as two or more alleles and which can therefore be used in genetic mapping.
An enzyme that synthesizes DNA on a DNA or RNA template.
A PCR technique that determines the alleles present at different STR loci within a genome in order to use DNA information to identify individuals.
Determination of the order of nucleotides in a DNA molecule.
Cleavage of a DNA molecule with two different restriction endonucleases, either concurrently or consecutively.
Separation of molecules on the basis of their charge‐to‐mass ratio.
A technique that identifies a DNA fragment that has a bound protein by virtue of its decreased mobility during gel electrophoresis.
A method for increasing DNA uptake by protoplasts through prior exposure to a high voltage, which results in the temporary formation of small pores in the cell membrane.
The unbinding of a molecule from a chromatography column.
A totipotent cell from the embryo of a mouse or other organism, used in construction of a transgenic animal such as a knockout mouse.
Conversion of a sticky end to a blunt end by enzymatic synthesis of the complement to the single‐stranded extension.
An enzyme that breaks phosphodiester bonds within a nucleic acid molecule.
A plasmid capable of integration into the host cell’s chromosome.
Precipitation of nucleic acid molecules by ethanol plus salt, used primarily as a means of concentrating DNA.
A fluorescent chemical that intercalates between base pairs in a double‐stranded DNA molecule, used in the detection of DNA.
An enzyme that sequentially removes nucleotides from the ends of a nucleic acid molecule.
The methodology used to identify the proteins in a proteome.
A cloning vector designed so that a foreign gene inserted into the vector is expressed in the host organism.
A vessel used for the large‐scale culture of microorganisms.
An electrophoresis technique for the separation of large DNA molecules.
A method for measuring DNA concentration with a DNA‐binding fluorophore.
An organic compound that emits fluorescent light when stimulated with light of a different wavelength.
The identification of a protein‐binding site on a DNA molecule by determining which phosphodiester bonds are protected from cleavage by deoxyribonuclease I.
The strategy by which the genes responsible for a phenotype are identified by determining which genes are inactivated in organisms that display a mutant version of that phenotype.
One of the two directions in which a double‐stranded DNA molecule can be sequenced.
Studies aimed at identifying all the genes in a genome and determining their expression patterns and functions.
A protein array designed to enable protein interactions to be studied.
A recombinant protein that carries a short peptide from the host organism at its amino or, less commonly, carboxyl terminus.
Electrophoresis performed in a gel matrix so that molecules of similar electric charge can be separated on the basis of size.
A technique that identifies a DNA fragment that has a bound protein by virtue of its decreased mobility during gel electrophoresis.
One of the two groups of DNA viruses that infect plants, the members of which have potential as cloning vectors for some species of higher plants.
A segment of DNA that codes for an RNA and/or polypeptide molecule.
A genetic engineering strategy that involves the introduction of a new gene or group of genes into an organism.

Insertion of a fragment of DNA, carrying a gene, into a cloning vector, and subsequent propagation of the recombinant DNA molecule in a host organism. Also used to describe those techniques that achieve the same result without the use of a cloning vector (e.g. direct gene transfer).
A method that enables directed changes to be made in a target gene.
A technique that results in inactivation of a gene, as a means of determining the function of that gene.
Determination of the relative positions of different genes on a DNA molecule.
A genetic engineering strategy that involves the inactivation of one or more of an organism’s genes.
A clinical procedure in which a gene or other DNA sequence is used to treat a disease.
A service that provides patients with guidance on the interpretation of genetic typing results.
The use of experimental techniques to produce DNA molecules containing new genes or new combinations of genes.
A hybridization technique that determines the genomic distribution of a hypervariable dispersed repetitive sequence and results in a banding pattern that is specific for each individual.
The branch of biology devoted to the study of genes.
The complete set of genes of an organism.
The process by which the genes, control sequences, and other interesting features are identified in a genome sequence.
A software package or online system for display of an annotated genome sequence.
Consists of all the DNA present in a single cell or group of cells.
A collection of clones sufficient in number to include all the genes of a particular organism.
The study of a genome, in particular the complete sequencing of a genome.
A type of gene therapy in which a fertilized egg is provided with a copy of the correct version of the defective gene and reimplanted into the mother.
A crop plant that has been engineered by gene addition or gene subtraction.
One of the major sequence classes of mitochondrial DNA pre-sent in the human population.
The removal of microorganisms from a culture, usually by centrifugation.
An enzyme that breaks base pairs in a double‐stranded DNA molecule.
A phage that is introduced into a host cell in conjunction with a related cloning vector, in order to provide enzymes required for replication of the cloning vector.
The use of a labelled nucleic acid molecule to identify related molecules by hybridization probing.
Possessing two different versions of the mitochondrial genome.
A DNA sequencing strategy which involves a pre‐sequencing phase during which the genome is broken into large fragments, which are cloned and each sequenced individually by the shotgun method.
A column chromatography method with high resolving power.
A type of melt analysis that enables a single nucleotide polymorphism to be detected in a PCR product.
Recombination between two homologous doublestranded DNA molecules, i.e. ones which share extensive nucleotide sequence similarity.

Refers to two genes from different organisms that have evolved from the same ancestral gene. Two homologous genes are usually sufficiently similar in sequence for one to be used as a hybridization probe for the other.
The version of gene editing that enables individual nucleotides in a target gene to be changed.
A technique in which genes with sequences similar to that of an unknown gene are sought, in order to confirm a gene identification or to understand the function of the unknown gene.

The attachment of a sequence of identical nucleotides (e.g. AAAAA) to the end of a nucleic acid molecule, usually referring to the synthesis of single‐stranded homopolymer extensions on the ends of a double‐stranded DNA molecule.
An enzyme that can be complexed to DNA and which is used in a non‐radioactive procedure for DNA labelling.
A mechanism by which some bacteria prevent phage attack through the synthesis of a restriction endonuclease that cleaves the non‐bacterial DNA.
A method used to identify the polypeptide coded by a cloned gene.
A labelled nucleic acid molecule that can be used to identify complementary or homologous molecules through the formation of stable base‐paired hybrids.
A method used to identify the polypeptide coded by a cloned gene.
The type of human repetitive DNA sequence used in genetic fingerprinting.
A next generation sequencing method utilizing reversible terminator sequencing of fragments immobilized on a slide.
The use of an antibody to detect a polypeptide synthesized by a cloned gene.
A technique for gene mapping involving hybridization of a labelled sample of a cloned gene to a large DNA molecule, usually a chromosome.
Any one of several techniques used to produce a specified mutation at a predetermined position in a DNA molecule.
Synthesis of infective λ particles from a preparation of λ capsid proteins and a concatemer of DNA molecules separated by cos sites.
A crystalline or paracrystalline deposit within a cell, often containing substantial quantities of insoluble protein.
Comprises a number of different types of plasmid, often related to each other, that are unable to coexist in the same cell.

A position where a DNA sequence has been inserted into or deleted from a genome, so called because it is impossible from comparison of two sequences to determine which alternative has occurred, insertion into one genome or deletion from the other.
(1) Of a gene: the switching on of the expression of a gene or group of genes in response to a chemical or other stimulus. (2) Of λ phage: the excision
of the integrated form of λ and accompanying switch to the lytic mode of infection, in response to a chemical or other stimulus.
A λ vector constructed by deleting a segment of non‐essential DNA.
A cloning strategy whereby insertion of a new piece of DNA into a vector inactivates a gene carried by the vector.
A method for separating molecules according to how tightly they bind to electrically charged particles present in a chromatographic matrix.
A next‐generation sequencing method that reads a sequence by detection of the hydrogen ions that are released every time a nucleotide is incorporated into the growing strand.
The component of an ion semiconductor sequencer that detects the hydrogen ions that are released during strand synthesis.
A next‐generation sequencing method that reads a sequence by detection of the hydrogen ions that are released every time a nucleotide is incorporated into the growing strand.
Separation of proteins in a gel that contains chemicals which establish a pH gradient when the electrical charge is applied.
The position in a pH gradient where the net charge of a protein is zero.
Markers, containing normal hydrogen or deuterium atoms, used to label individual proteomes.
The part of the centromere to which spindle microtubules attach.
An examination of DNA profiles or other information to determine if two individuals are related.
A DNA polymerase enzyme, obtained by chemical modification of E. coli DNA polymerase I.
A mouse that has been engineered so that it carries an inactivated gene.
The incorporation of a marker nucleotide into a nucleic acid molecule. The marker is often, but not always, a radioactive or fluorescent label.

A means of identifying recombinant bacteria containing vectors that carry the lacZ′ gene. The bacteria are plated on a medium that contains an analogue of lactose that gives a blue colour in the presence of β‐galactosidase activity.
A bacteriophage that infects E. coli, derivatives of which are used as cloning vectors.
(1) A collections of clones, e.g. a genomic library. (2) A collection of DNA fragments prepared for sequencing by a next-generation method.
An enzyme that, in the cell, repairs single‐stranded discontinuities in double‐stranded DNA molecules. Purified DNA ligase is used in gene cloning to join DNA molecules together.
A technique for mapping the chromosomal position of a gene by comparing its inheritance pattern with that of genes and other loci whose map positions are already known.
A synthetic, double‐stranded oligonucleotide used to attach sticky ends to a blunt‐ended molecule.
A lipid vesicle sometimes used to introduce DNA into an animal or plant cell.
A bacterium that harbours a prophage.
The pattern of phage infection that involves integration of the phage DNA into the host chromosome.
An enzyme that weakens the cell walls of certain types of bacteria.

The pattern of infection displayed by a phage that replicates and lyses the host cell immediately after the initial infection. Integration of the phage DNA molecule into the bacterial chromosome does not occur.
A bacteriophage that infects E. coli, derivatives of which are used as cloning vectors.
A high‐throughput sequencing strategy in which many individual sequences are generated in parallel.
An analytical technique in which ions are separated according to their mass‐to‐charge ratios.
A type of mass spectrometry used in proteomics.
A method used to detect the presence of single nucleotide polymorphisms in a PCR product.
The temperature at which a double‐stranded DNA or DNA–RNA molecule denatures.
The transcript of a protein‐coding gene.
A set of genes or cDNAs immobilized on a glass slide and used in transcriptome studies.
A method of introducing new DNA into a cell by injecting it directly into the nucleus.
A polymorphism comprising tandem copies of, usually, two‐, three‐, four‐ or five‐nucleotide repeat units. Also called a short tandem repeat (STR).
A defined medium that provides only the minimum number of different nutrients needed for growth of a particular bacterium.
The DNA molecules present in the mitochondria of eukaryotes.
The woman who lived in Africa between 140 000 and 290 000 years ago and who carried the ancestral mitochondrial DNA that gave rise to all the mitochondrial DNAs in existence today.
A technique that uses chemical modification to identify nucleotides involved in interactions with a DNA‐binding protein.
An analysis based on the inferred mutation rate that enables times to be assigned to the branch points in a phylogenetic tree.
A characteristic that is specified by a single gene.
A plasmid with a high copy number.
A number of identical or related genes present in the same organism, usually coding for a family of related polypeptides.
A directed evolution strategy that involves taking parts of each member of a multigene family and reassembling these parts to create new gene variants.
A PCR carried out with more than one pair of primers and hence targeting two or more sites in the DNA being studied
A hypothesis that holds that modern humans in the Old World are descended from Homo erectus populations that left Africa over one million years ago.
A measure of the degree of completeness of a genome sequence based on the total length of contigs or scaffolds.
A method for DNA sequencing without the use of a DNA polymerase.
A collection of DNA sequencing methods, each involving a massively parallel strategy.
A measure of the degree of completeness of a genome sequence that takes account of the actual size of the genome.
A single‐strand break, involving the absence of one or more nucleotides, in a double‐stranded DNA molecule.
The repair of a nick with DNA polymerase I, usually to introduce labelled nucleotides into a DNA molecule.
A technique for transferring bands of RNA from an agarose gel to a nitrocellulose or nylon membrane.
A technique, used in the production of transgenic animals, that involves transfer of the nucleus of a somatic cell into an oocyte whose own nucleus has been removed.
Formation of a double‐stranded molecule by base pairing between complementary or homologous polynucleotides.
A short, synthetic, single‐stranded DNA molecule, such as one used as a primer in DNA sequencing or PCR.
An in vitro mutagenesis technique that involves the use of a synthetic oligonucleotide to introduce the predetermined nucleotide alteration into the gene to be mutated.
The non‐supercoiled conformation taken up by a circular double‐stranded DNA molecule when one or both polynucleotides carry nicks.
A series of codons that is or could be a gene.
A parameter used to measure the growth of a bacterial culture.
A method for increasing DNA uptake by protoplasts through prior exposure to a laser, which results in the temporary formation of small pores in the cell membrane.
Examination of a DNA sequence for open reading frames in order to locate the genes.
The specific position on a DNA molecule where DNA replication begins.
An open reading frame thought to be a functional gene but to which no function has yet been assigned.
A gel electrophoresis technique that employs a pulsed electric field to achieve separation of very large molecules of DNA.
A hypothesis that holds that modern humans evolved in Africa, moving to the rest of the Old World and displacing the descendants of Homo erectus that they encountered.
A transposon from Drosophila melanogaster used as the basis of a cloning vector for that organism.
A bacteriophage that infects E. coli, derivatives of which are used as cloning vectors.
A cloning vector based on the P1 bac teriophage, used for cloning relatively large fragments of DNA in E. coli.
A version of single‐molecule real‐time DNA sequencing.
A group of mammalian viruses, derivatives of which have been used as cloning vectors.
Treatment of a DNA molecule with a restriction endonuclease under such conditions that only a fraction of all the recognition sites are cleaved.
The use of a human family tree to analyse the inheritance of a genetic or DNA marker.
Identification of a protein by examination of the mass spectrometric properties of peptides generated by treatment with a sequence‐specific protease.

The use of individual genome sequences to make accurate diagnoses of a person’s risk of developing a disease, and the use of that person’s genetic characteristics to plan effective therapies and treatment regimes.
A technique involving cloning in M13 that is used to identify proteins that interact with one another.
A collection of M13 clones carrying different DNA fragments, used in phage display.
A double‐stranded plasmid vector that possesses an origin of replication from a filamentous phage and hence can be used to synthesize a single‐stranded version of a cloned gene.
Genetic modification of a farm animal so that the animal synthesizes a recombinant pharmaceutical protein, often in its milk.
A type of plate radiography that can be used to image the positions of radioactive label in an electrophoresis gel.
A technique that uses pulses of light to construct an oligonucleotide from light‐activated nucleotide substrates.
One of the structures present on the surface of a bacterium containing a conjugative plasmid, through which DNA is thought to pass during conjugation.
A zone of clearing on a lawn of bacteria caused by lysis of the cells by infecting phage particles.
A usually circular piece of DNA, primarily independent of the host chromosome, often found in bacteria and some other types of cells.
A method involving incubation with an inhibitor of protein synthesis aimed at increasing the copy number of certain types of plasmid in a bacterial culture.
A polymeric compound used to precipitate macromolecules and molecular aggregates.
A synthetic double‐stranded oligonucleotide carrying a number of restriction sites.
A technique that enables multiple copies of a DNA molecule to be generated by enzymatic amplification of a target DNA sequence.
Refers to a locus that is present as a number of different alleles or other variations in the population as a whole.
A procedure that uses information on the map position of a gene to obtain a clone of that gene.
Refers to the variations in expression levels observed for genes inserted at different positions in a genome.
Studies aimed at identifying all the genes in a genome and determining their expression patterns and functions.

A short single‐stranded oligonucleotide which, when attached by base pairing to a single‐stranded template molecule, acts as the start point for complementary strand synthesis directed by a DNA polymerase enzyme.
A method of transcript analysis in which the 5′ end of an RNA is mapped by annealing and extending an oligonucleotide primer.
Refers to the amount of DNA synthesis that is carried out by a DNA polymerase before dissociation from the template.
A virus infection cycle that is able to proceed to completion and result in synthesis and release of new virus particles.
The nucleotide sequence, upstream of a gene, that acts as a signal for RNA polymerase binding.
The 3′ to 5′ exonuclease activity possessed by some DNA polymerases which enables the enzyme to replace a misincorporated nucleotide.
The integrated form of the DNA molecule of a lysogenic phage.
A protein from the bacterium Staphylococcus aureus that binds specifically to immunoglobulin G (i.e. antibody) molecules.
Separation of proteins in an electrophoresis gel.

A collection of techniques, including but not exclusively in vitro mutagenesis, that result in directed alterations being made to protein molecules, often to improve the properties of enzymes used in industrial processes.
The methodology used to identify the proteins in a proteome.
The entire protein content of a cell or tissue.
The collection of techniques used to study the proteome.
A cell from which the cell wall has been completely removed.
A gel electrophoresis technique that employs a pulsed electric field to achieve separation of very large molecules of DNA.
A DNA sequencing method in which addition of a nucleotide to the end of a growing polynucleotide is detected directly by conversion of the released pyrophosphate into a flash of chemiluminescence.
A method for quantifying the amount of product synthesized during a test PCR by comparison with the amounts synthesized during PCRs with known amounts of starting DNA.
A PCR‐based technique for mapping the end of an RNA molecule.
A radioactive atom used in the detection of a larger molecule into which it has been incorporated.
A method for DNA labelling that utilizes random DNA hexamers, which anneal to single‐stranded DNA and act as primers for complementary strand synthesis by a suitable enzyme.
A single sequence from the output of a next‐generation sequencing run.
One of the six overlapping sequences of triplet codons, three on each polynucleotide, contained in a segment of a DNA double helix.
A modification of the standard PCR technique in which synthesis of the product is measured as the PCR proceeds through its series of cycles.
A transformed cell that contains a recombinant DNA molecule.
A DNA molecule created in the test tube by ligating together pieces of DNA that are not normally contiguous.
All of the techniques involved in the construction, study, and use of recombinant DNA molecules.
A polypeptide that is synthesized in a recombinant cell as the result of expression of a cloned gene.
The exchange of DNA sequences between different molecules, occurring either naturally or as a result of DNA manipulation.
An existing genome sequence that is used to aid assembly of the reads obtained by next-generation sequencing of a related genome.
(1) Refers to a plasmid with a high copy number of perhaps 50 or more per cell. (2) The non‐supercoiled conformation of open‐circular DNA.
A λ vector designed so that insertion of new DNA is by replacement of part of the non‐essential region of the λ DNA molecule.
A technique whereby the colonies on an agar plate are transferred en masse to a new plate, on which the colonies grow in the same relative positions as before.
The double‐stranded form of the M13 DNA molecule found within infected E. coli cells.
A gene whose phenotype can be assayed in a transformed organism, and which is used in, for example, deletion analyses of regulatory regions.
A short oligonucleotide that gives a fluorescent signal when it hybridizes with a target DNA.
The switching off of expression of a gene or a group of genes in response to a chemical or other stimulus.
Determination of the number and sizes of the DNA fragments produced when a particular DNA molecule is cut with a particular restriction endonuclease.
An endonuclease that cuts DNA molecules only at a limited number of specific nucleotide sequences.
A mutation that results in alteration of a restriction site and hence a change in the pattern of fragments obtained when a DNA molecule is cut with a restriction endonuclease.
A map showing the positions of different restriction sites in a DNA molecule.
A virus with an RNA genome, able to insert into a host chromosome, derivatives of which have been used to clone genes in mammalian cells.
The strategy by which the function of a gene is identified by mutating that gene and identifying the phenotypic change that results.
A column chromatography method that separates proteins according to their degree of surface hydrophobicity.
One of the two directions in which a double‐stranded DNA molecule can be sequenced.
An RNA‐dependent DNA polymerase, able to synthesize a complementary DNA molecule on a template of single‐stranded RNA.
A PCR technique in which the starting material is RNA. The first step in the procedure is conversion of the RNA to cDNA with reverse transcriptase.
A DNA sequencing method in which the sequence is read by detection of the fluorescent label attached to each nucleotide that is added to a growing polynucleotide.

A technique that uses a closely linked RFLP as a marker for the presence of a particular allele in a DNA sample, often as a means of screening individuals for a defective gene responsible for a genetic disease.
The short nucleotide sequence upstream of a gene, which after transcription forms the site on the mRNA molecule to which the ribosome binds.
A method for RNA transcript mapping.
A gene carried by a vector and conferring a recognizable characteristic on a cell containing the vector or a recombinant DNA molecule derived from the vector.
A means of obtaining a clone containing a desired recombinant DNA molecule.
Assembly of the many short reads obtained by nextgeneration sequencing into a contiguous DNA sequence.
A contiguous DNA sequence obtained as an intermediate in a genome sequencing project.
The average number of reads that cover each nucleotide position in a DNA sequence obtained by a next-generation method.
A DNA sequence whose position has been mapped in a genome.
A method for studying the composition of a transcriptome.
A polymorphism comprising tandem copies of, usually, two‐, three‐, four‐ or five‐nucleotide repeat units. Also called a microsatellite.
A genome sequencing strategy in which the molecules to be sequenced are randomly broken into fragments which are then individually sequenced.
A cloning strategy that involves the insertion of random fragments of a large DNA molecule into a vector, resulting in a large number of different recombinant DNA molecules.
A vector that can replicate in the cells of more than one organism (e.g. in E. coli and in yeast).
A mammalian virus that has been used as the basis for a cloning vector.
A third‐generation DNA sequencing method which uses an advanced optical system to observe the addition of individual nucleotides to a growing polynucleotide.
A point mutation that is carried by some individuals of a population.
Techniques used to produce a specified mutation at a predetermined position in a DNA molecule.
A type of gene therapy in which the correct version of a gene is introduced into a somatic cell.
A procedure that uses ultrasound to cause random breaks in DNA molecules.
A method for increasing DNA uptake by protoplasts through prior exposure to ultrasound, which results in the temporary formation of small pores in the cell membrane.
A technique for transferring bands of DNA from an agarose gel to a nitrocellulose or nylon membrane.
A cell with a partially degraded cell wall.
A method for accelerating ion‐exchange chromatography by centrifuging the chromatography column.
The relaxation of the specificity of a restriction endonuclease that sometimes occurs when the reaction is carried out under non‐optimal conditions, e.g. in a low‐salt buffer.
A hairpin structure, consisting of a base‐paired stem and a nonbase‐paired loop, that may form in a polynucleotide.
An end of a double‐stranded DNA molecule where there is a singlestranded extension.
Refers to a plasmid with a low copy number of perhaps just one or two per cell.
An efficient promoter that can direct synthesis of RNA transcripts at a relatively fast rate.
Computer methods that attempt to predict the structure and/or function of a protein or a protein domain from its amino acid sequence.
The part of a λ replacement vector that is removed during insertion of new DNA.
